 Trump praises Hegseth on Veterans Day after House blocks impeachment effort
 By Alejandra Jaramillo 
 President Donald Trump praised Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during his Veterans Day remarks at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, a day after the House blocked an effort to impeach him.
 “The Secretary of War, Peter Hegseth,” Trump said, which drew loud applause from the crowd.
 “I had a feeling that was going to happen. He’s done a fantastic job, but he loves you and he protects you. This is all about you,” Trump said after opening his remarks by thanking those who have served.
 “On Veterans Day, we reaffirm our undying gratitude to every neighbor who has answered the call of duty,” Trump said.
 The White House has publicly backed Hegseth and worked behind the scenes to defeat the impeachment push from outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie.

 Catch up: Future House Oversight Committee chair rebukes White House investigation warning
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 A day after an impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was foiled, the White House has warned the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee that the Trump administration “will not be extorted,” cautioning against forthcoming congressional investigations.
 Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, offered a strong rebuke of the White House’s warning, saying: “It appears Donald Trump has something to hide.”
 Here’s what else has been going on: 
 A local county election board in Mississippi has finally announced the number of provisional ballots still to count , as Hinds County — one of the state’s most populous — has taken days to go through accepting and rejecting these ballots.
 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there is “zero change” in the administration’s immigration policy , even after President Donald Trump indicated he would be open to a deal that allows for amnesty for some people living in the country illegally.
 Senate Democrats will hold their leadership elections on December 1 , according to a Senate Democratic aide. House Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections next week.
 Democrat Raymond Smith will flip North Carolina’s 3rd District , CNN’s Decision Desk projects, unseating GOP Rep. Greg Murphy, who has held the seat since 2019.
 Former UN Ambassador Nikki Haley, who ran in the Republican primary in 2024, has said she will not run for president in 2028. 
 CNN’s Alejandra Jaramillo, Michael Williams, Lauren Fox, Annie Grayer, Manu Raju, Bruna Horvath, Ethan Cohen and Katherine Koretski contributed to this reporting.

 Fox News puts Mullin on defensive over potential amnesty deal
 By Michael Williams 
 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there is “zero change” in the administration’s immigration policy, even after President Donald Trump indicated he would be open to a deal that allows for amnesty for some people living in the country illegally.
 Mullin was pressed by Fox News Channel host Laura Ingraham Tuesday over Trump’s expressing receptiveness during an interview with “60 Minutes” to a deal with the new, Democrat-led Congress that could involve amnesty for people who have worked in the US for years while living here illegally. His comments drew criticism from immigration hardliners on the right who said it ran counter to his campaign promises.
 “Can you promise our viewers, and the 77 million people who voted for President Trump, that there is no change in his immigration policy?” Ingraham asked Mullin.
 The secretary responded: “Zero change. The president made that very clear. We’re still going after the worst of the worst and amnesty will never be on the table.”
 Ingraham then asked how Mullin was going to keep the administration’s promise of deporting millions “if we keep hearing this inching toward, well, maybe we’ll make a deal?”
 “Because I’m going to tell you, the Trump base, the people who made this reality, this administration a reality, they do not want you to let up at all,” she told Mullin.
 Mullin said Trump maintains his veto control and “will not sign anything that isn’t in the right movement for this country and the Republican Party.”

 Nikki Haley says she won't run for president in 2028
 By Katherine Koretski 
 Nikki Haley walks on stage at her caucus night event on January 15, 2024 in West Des Moines, Iowa. 
 Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images 
 Former UN Ambassador Nikki Haley said she will not run for president in 2028.
 During an interview with CNBC on Wednesday, Haley, who ran in the Republican primary in 2024, said:
 “I am not running in 2028, but I will continue to talk about the things that I care about. I will continue to push good policy. I will continue to support good candidates, and we want a strong America.”
 Haley didn’t close the door on serving as a Republican delegate on the campaign trail, adding, “Whatever we have to do, I think every one of us has an obligation to try and continue those moving the ball forward.”
 The former governor of South Carolina wouldn’t say who she would throw her support behind on the GOP side, but she did say that Democrats have a leg up following last week’s midterms.
 “They have a very talented slate on the Democrat side. We have the possibility of a talented slate on the Republican side. The question is, which party learns the lessons going into 2028? Because American people are very smart, and they’re going to decide based on who they trust,” she said.
 She also emphasized what she sees as a Republican identity crisis: “I don’t want to see a Democrat president. What I do want to see is Republicans go back to remembering who we are and what we believe in.”
 “Let’s start talking about the issues and stop hating on each other. I’m all for Republicans being strong Republicans, but what Americans don’t want is the hate and the back-and-forth. They want results. We’ve got to give it to them. We owe it,” she continued.
 Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images, Sean Gallup/Getty Images, Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images, Eric Lee/Pool/Reuters, Alex Wong/Getty Images, Andrew Harnik/Getty Images, CNN

 Hinds County election board announces number of provisional and absentee ballots left
 By Annie Grayer 
 Hinds County Election Commission Chair Yvonne R. Horton holds a sheet of paper while working at a computer as election observers stand behind her at the Hinds County Election Operations Center in Jackson, Mississippi, on November 9, 2026, with the US Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith still too close to call. 
 Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty Images 
 A local county election board in Mississippi has finally announced the number of provisional ballots still to count as Hinds County — one of the state’s most populous — has taken days to go through accepting and rejecting these ballots.
 Officials have accepted 817 ballots and rejected 1,609 affidavit ballots. Ballots were rejected for a variety of reasons including if a voter didn’t have the proper identification, voted in the wrong precinct or couldn’t be located in the poll book.
 Officials will also count 67 mail-in absentee ballots that were received by Hinds County postmarked Election Day and received by November 10.
 These ballots are critical to the Senate race that still remains too close to call.

 Garcia says Congress has "wide latitude to conduct investigations"
 By Lauren Fox 
 Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, offered a strong rebuke of the White House counsel’s letter alleging that some of the California Democrat’s forthcoming investigations may be crossing a line and even amount to illegal action.
 “It appears Donald Trump has something to hide,” Garcia said in a statement Wednesday morning. “Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate.”
 The response comes as House Democrats are preparing to unfurl a series of investigations targeting the president, his administration and their connections to various corporations.
 The work will be undertaken by several congressional committees, but the House Oversight Committee is likely to be the tip of the investigative spear for Democrats.
 “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse. The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers,” Garcia said.

 Democrat Raymond Smith will flip North Carolina’s 3rd District, CNN projects
 By Bruna Horvath and Ethan Cohen 
 Democrat Raymond Smith will flip North Carolina’s 3rd district, CNN’s Decision Desk projects.
 He will unseat GOP Rep. Greg Murphy, who has held the seat since 2019.
 Smith took a narrow 293-vote lead Tuesday after provisional ballots were counted, and while the race is likely to end close enough that Murphy could request a recount, he conceded the race Wednesday and his chief of staff confirmed to CNN he would not call for one.
 Smith is an Army veteran and educator who ran on issues like affordability and strengthening public education.
 His win is part of a blue wave this midterm election cycle, with Democrats regaining control of the House of Representatives and Senate. CNN projected on election night that Roy Cooper, North Carolina’s popular former Democratic governor, would win the state’s open Senate seat.

 White House tells Garcia it "will not be extorted" in letter warning about oversight
 By Alejandra Jaramillo and Michael Williams 
 Rep. Robert Garcia gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House office building in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. 
 Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images 
 The White House has warned the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee that the Trump administration “will not be extorted” as it cautions against forthcoming congressional investigations.
 “The Trump Administration expects members of Congress to discharge their investigative functions within settled constitutional limits,” said the White House letter to Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, which was obtained by CNN and dated Monday. According to a source familiar with the matter, however, Garcia has not received the letter from the White House.
 “The Administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government.”
 The letter signed by White House counsel Will Scharf also states that threatening executive branch officials to discourage them from public service could amount to “blatant criminality.”
 Scharf goes on to say that congressional investigations “must further a legitimate legislative task” and “Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary.”
 Garcia has vowed to take an “aggressive” oversight approach, despite Trump pushing his administration to look into Democrats who are investigating him. As the midterm results became clear last week, Garcia posted on X : “LAWYER UP.”
 “The days of us not fighting back are over. This idea that we’re every single time not going to actually take on that fight is over. We’ve got to be in the fight and be aggressive,” Garcia told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union” over the weekend.
 The California Democrat accused Attorney General Todd Blanche of “threatening” lawmakers on the panel with investigations in an attempt to stop them from conducting oversight, adding, “they can come after us however they want. We’re not going to be intimidated.”
 This post has been updated with additional information. CNN’s Annie Grayer contributed to this report.

 US-bound migrants in Mexico hopeful after US midterm results - despite US warnings 
 0:54
 Hundreds of people from South and Central America are walking from southern Mexico to the north of the country, in the hope that the historic Democratic win in last week’s midterms means that US border controls are eased.
 The people are walking despite the fact that, two days after Election Day, the American Embassy in El Salvador posted a stern reminder on social media:
 “US immigration laws remain in effect,” the Spanish-language post read. “The midterm election results do not represent changes to current immigration policies.”

 House Republican uneasy about GOP's post-election moves
 By Alison Main and Manu Raju 
 House Republicans were divided after Rep. Jim Jordan, a Trump ally and firebrand, emerged as the winner of a closed-door meeting to vote on the next leader of their conference.
 Rep. David Joyce said he talked to both Jordan and Scalise before Tuesday’s leadership election and warned, “we can’t double down on stupid” when asked what message was sent with the ascendance of Jordan and Stephen Miller into powerful roles. Miller is the new White House Chief of Staff.
 “What happened to us was a message clear and very loud that people don’t like the way we’re been moving in the wrong direction, and you can’t lie to people about the things that they feel,” he said, urging Republicans to “create a plan of action to move forward.”
 Asked if he voted for Jordan to be GOP leader, Joyce responded, “I support the ticket has been elected.”
 Rep. Tom McClintock of California said he was “ecstatic” after Jordan’s win.
 Asked if he was ok with Jordan aligning himself with Trump, McClintock responded, “my loyalty’s never been to an individual; it’s always been to the principles of the American founding, which are also the principles of the Republican Party. We’ve always done best when we’ve adhered to those principles.”
 Rep. Brian Mast said he thought Jordan was “our best messenger.”
 “If you look at our conference; we’re a significantly more conservative conference than what we were coming into this, and I think if you look at that, you’re going to see us push our conservative values,” he told CNN.

 Democrats say they would have lost impeachment vote despite absences
 By Sarah Ferris 
 Democrats lost a vote on Tuesday night that would have triggered an impeachment vote on Pete Hegseth because, in part, several of their own members were stuck in traffic.
 But Democrats have pointed out that they would have lost the vote anyways, even if those members did make it to the floor for the vote.
 Because Republicans control the floor, they could have held open the vote as long as possible for their own members — some of whom also missed the vote — to arrive.
 Another vote later on Tuesday night proved that Republicans did have members in town who missed the first vote. The final vote, if all those members had made it to the floor, however, would have still failed 216 to 215.
 Only one Republican — Trump critic Rep. Thomas Massie who introduced impeachment articles against Hegseth — voted in favor of advancing the impeachment vote.
 Both parties had been initially expecting more GOP defections after last week’s midterm election losses.

 Roughly 75% of Americans will have Democratic governors
 By Eric Bradner 
 As soon as this year’s winners are sworn in, roughly 75% of all Americans will have Democratic governors — a shakeup that reflects the party’s dominance in the nation’s most populous states and could have a seismic impact on everything from redistricting and the Electoral College to health care and tax policies, education funding and more.
 At least 28 states will now have Democratic governors. It will be 29 if Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher wins the still-uncalled race in Kansas — extending for a third term the party’s governorship of a state that votes reliably red in presidential races.
 Alaska, where votes are still being counted , could become the 30th Democratic win.
 Democrats also won several key downballot statewide offices and gained hundreds of seats in state legislative chambers across the country.
 Democrats will hold the governor’s offices in 13 of the 14 most populated states — including Texas , the biggest prize of all in the 2026 midterm elections. In addition to the Lone Star State, Democrats also flipped the GOP-held governorships in Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada — and could soon add Alaska to that list.
 Republicans retain the job in just one big state: Florida. After that, the next-largest states with Republican governors, by population, are Tennessee, Indiana and Missouri.

 Here's how House members voted on the impeachment of Pete Hegseth
 By Jedd Rosche , Becky Pinnington and Curt Merrill 
 The House of Representatives voted yesterday evening to send an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively killing the movement to oust the defense secretary before the end of the year.
 The vote was 211-204. While Republicans will still be in charge of both chambers until the new Congress is sworn in January, Democrats in part gave House GOP leaders a window to sideline the impeachment effort due to absences. Eleven House Democrats did not vote on the measure, more than the seven-vote margin.
 Some of the Democrats were unable to be there due to a traffic incident. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, meanwhile, was in San Francisco for a Veterans Day event. 
 Seven House Republicans also did not vote on the measure which was led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky – the only Republican member to vote against tabling the measure.
 Here’s an overview of how the votes went. Red dots represent Republican votes, blue dots represent Democrat votes, and the yellow dot represents independent California Rep. Kevin Kiley.
 You can see the full list of names here .

 A CNN poll on 2028 contenders shows how wide-open the next election is
 Analysis by Zachary B. Wolf 
 64% of CNN poll respondents are 'taking more of a wait-and-see attitude' as to who will be next into the White House. 
 Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images 
 If the 2026 midterms were an opportunity for voters to express their feelings about President Donald Trump’s administration, the election in two years will be their first opportunity to cast a vote for president without his name on the ballot.
 Trump is constitutionally barred from running again, which means, as the lame duck portion of his presidency comes into view, it’s not too early to start thinking about who might replace him.
 A little more than half of Americans, 54%, have given at least some thought to the coming presidential race, according to a CNN Poll conducted by SSRS in the month before the midterm election. Fewer, 40%, said they’re looking forward to it, with 27% saying they’re dreading it and the rest expressing neither outlook.
 About a third of Americans, 35%, said there’s a specific candidate they’d like to see run, compared to 64% who are taking more of a wait-and-see attitude.
 No major candidate has yet declared a campaign, although the first of those could come sooner than many people think.

 Here's what's on Trump's schedule this Veterans Day
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House, on November 5. 
 Alex Brandon/AP 
 President Donald Trump is set to participate in the 73rd annual National Veterans Day Observance today.
 Here’s a look at what’s on his schedule: 
 At 8 a.m. ET, Trump is expected to participate in Executive Time.
 After this, he is set to travel to Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.
 At 10:20 a.m. ET, there will be a wreath laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, followed by a performance by the US Coast Guard Band and the US Air Force Singing Sergeants.
 At 11 a.m. ET, observance and a parade of colors will take place in the Memorial Amphitheater.
 Half an hour later, Trump is scheduled to deliver Veterans Day Remarks.
 The president is then scheduled to travel back to the White House.

 What to know about Jim Jordan, the hardline conservative selected as House minority leader
 By Ellis Kim 
 Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, talks with reporters in the Capitol Visitor Center after he won the position of minority leader for the 120th Congress in the House Republican leadership elections on Tuesday. 
 Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc./Getty Images 
 House Republicans have picked Rep. Jim Jordan — the famously pugnacious pro-Trump fighter — to l ead their party in the minority next year, according to multiple sources familiar. The vote was 106 to 73.
 Republicans have chosen one of the party’s most aggressive and combative figures as the face of their party, a clear sign that they are ready for battle — not compromise — with Democrats next year.
 Jordan has served as chair of the powerful House Judiciary committee since 2023. A fierce and longtime ally of President Donald Trump, Jordan has used his gavel and his seat on the oversight panel to probe what he has argued is the weaponization of the government against the president.
 The Ohio Republican, who was first elected to Congress in 2007, has also long been an influential voice in the GOP conference. He helped found the House Freedom Caucus in 2015, leading the right-wing bloc that rankled former Speaker John Boehner before he resigned from Congress.
 While the group’s members have maintained a reputation for frustrating House GOP leaders and thwarting legislation, Jordan has more recently taken a more deferential approach and aligned himself closely with Republican Speakers Kevin McCarthy and Mike Johnson.
 Many of Jordan’s colleagues have long believed the former state legislator and college wrestling coach was hungry for a greater leadership role. Some saw his prolific campaigning for House Republican candidates this year as an effort to lay the groundwork for a potential minority leader run.
 Jordan made a bid for the speaker’s gavel after McCarthy’s ouster in 2023. But he faced opposition from some moderates and Steve Scalise allies and failed to get the votes on the floor.
 CNN”s Sarah Ferris, Manu Raju and Annie Grayer contributed to this reporting.

 What is an article of impeachment?
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 Rep. Thomas Massie, speaks outside of the Capitol about articles of impeachment he introduced against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday. 
 Allison Robbert/AP 
 An article of impeachment is a “documented written statement of charges relied upon as the basis for removing an individual from office,” according to Cornell Law School. 
 It is the “constitutional equivalent of an indictment, which are used in common criminal cases,” the school says.
 GOP Rep Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment this week, accusing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of waging war in Iran without congressional approval, ignoring laws about minimizing civilian casualties and directing the Defense Department to carry out extrajudicial killings.
 The attempt was foiled when House Republican leaders convinced enough from the party to show up to the vote, with a 211 representatives voting to kill the impeachment effort and 204 voting to sustain it. 11 Democrats and seven Republicans missed the vote.
 Once impeachment articles are brought about in the House of Representatives, they are voted on. If the articles are adopted by a majority, the official they are levied against is impeached.
 After this, the House will send the articles of impeachment to the Senate. The Senate then sits as a High Court of Impeachment “to consider evidence, hear witnesses, and vote to acquit or convict the impeached official,” according to the United States Senate website.

 These are the 11 Democrats who missed the vote that killed the Hegseth impeachment effort
 By Jedd Rosche 
 Members of the US Congress arrive for a procedural vote on whether to send the potential impeachment of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, on Capitol Hill last night. 
 Jonathan Ernst/Reuters 
 The House voted on Tuesday evening to send the effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, essentially killing the push led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie this Congress.
 Tuesday’s tally was 211-204, meaning Republicans were successful in part due to 11 House Democrats not being present for the vote. They were:
 Julia Brownley of California
 Lou Correa of California
 Laura Gillen of New York
 Steven Horsford of Nevada
 Jonathan Jackson of Illinois
 Nancy Pelosi of California
 Brittany Pettersen of Colorado
 Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico
 Haley Stevens of Michigan
 Marilyn Strickland of Washington
 Frederica Wilson of Florida
 Some of the Democrats were unable to be there due to a traffic incident. Former House Speaker Pelosi , meanwhile, was in San Francisco for a Veterans Day event.
 Rep. Pettersen said in a statement after the vote that Democrats would “impeach Hegseth” next year “and neither (Mike) Johnson nor (Donald) Trump will be able to stop us.”
 Seven House Republicans also missed Tuesday’s vote. They were:
 Monica De La Cruz of Texas
 Neal Dunn of Florida
 Russell Fry of South Carolina
 Julia Letlow of Louisiana
 Tom Tiffany of Wisconsin
 Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin
 Rudy Yakym of Indiana
